posts.topic: Finishing seam edges: zigzag, pinking, French seams

slides.title: 3 easy ways to finish your seams
slides.subtitle: Stop fraying in its tracks and make the inside of your garment look as good as the outside.

slides.title: Zigzag the edges
slides.body: No overlocker? No problem. Sew a medium zigzag along each raw edge of the seam allowance so the stitches wrap the edge and stop it fraying.

slides.title: Pinking shears
slides.body: Trim the seam allowance with pinking shears. The little zigzag cut slows fraying on stable woven cottons. It's quick, but best for garments that won't be washed constantly.

slides.title: The French seam
slides.body: Sew wrong sides together, trim close, then fold and sew again with right sides together. The raw edges are sealed inside. Perfect for sheer and lightweight fabrics.

slides.title: Save this for sewing day
slides.body: Our step-by-step instructions guide you through every seam, from the first stitch to the final press.

posts.topic: Finding the right side of the fabric using the selvedge

slides.title: Can't tell the right side? Check the selvedge
slides.body: Run a finger along the tiny holes in the selvedge. The side where they feel raised is usually the right side. Printed selvedge text often reads correctly on the right side too.

posts.caption_ig:
Plain fabric, both sides look the same... so which one is the right side? 🤔

Check the selvedge. The little holes along the edge are usually punched from the wrong side, so on the right side they feel slightly raised.

If your selvedge has printed text, it often reads correctly on the right side too ✨

Still can't tell? Pick one side, mark it with chalk and stay consistent on every piece.

Did you know this one? 👇

#sewingtips #fabric #sewingforbeginners #sewinghacks #isew
posts.caption_fb:
Quick fabric tip: can't tell the right side of your fabric? 🤔

posts.topic: Understanding ease: body measurements vs finished garment measurements

slides.title: What is ease, and why does it matter?
slides.subtitle: The secret behind patterns that feel comfortable, not tight. Here's how to read it before you pick your size.

slides.title: Body measurements come first
slides.body: The size chart lists body measurements: your bust, waist and hip. Measure yourself and find your size from XS to XL using US or UK sizing.

slides.title: Ease is the extra room
slides.body: The finished garment is bigger than your body so you can move, breathe and sit. That difference is called ease. A coat needs more ease than a fitted dress.

slides.title: Compare with a favourite
slides.body: Lay a garment you love flat and measure it. Compare with the pattern piece, minus seam allowances, to choose a little more or less ease.

slides.title: Find your perfect fit
slides.body: Every pattern includes sizes XS–XL with US and UK sizing and a clear size chart.

posts.caption_ig:
Ever sewn your exact size and it still felt too tight, or way too roomy? Meet ease 📏

Ease is the extra room between your body and the finished garment. It's what lets you move, sit and breathe.

Swipe for how to use it: start with your body measurements, understand the extra room, then compare with a garment you already love.
